{{Short description|Problem in quantum information science}}
{{Broader|Quantum simulator}}
'''Hamiltonian simulation''' (also referred to as '''quantum simulation''') is a problem in [[quantum information science]] that attempts to find the [[computational complexity]] and [[Quantum algorithm|quantum algorithms]] needed for simulating quantum systems. Hamiltonian simulation is a problem that demands algorithms which implement the evolution of a [[quantum state]] efficiently. The Hamiltonian simulation problem was proposed by [[Richard Feynman]] in 1982, where he proposed a [[quantum computer]] as a possible solution since the simulation of general Hamiltonians seem to grow exponentially with respect to the system size.<ref name=Feynman1982>{{Cite journal
 | title = Simulating physics with computers
 | url = https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02650179
 | year = 1982
 | author = Richard P Feynman
 | journal = International Journal of Theoretical Physics
 | pages = 467–488
 | volume = 21
 | issue = 6
 | access-date = 2019-05-04
 | bibcode = 1982IJTP...21..467F
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02650179
 | s2cid = 124545445
 | url-access = subscription
 }}</ref>

== Problem statement ==
In the Hamiltonian simulation problem, given a [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] <math>H</math> (<math>2^n \times 2^n</math> [[hermitian matrix]] acting on <math>n</math> qubits), a time <math>t</math> and maximum simulation error <math>\epsilon</math>, the goal is to find an algorithm that approximates <math> U </math> such that <math>||U - e^{-iHt} || \leq \epsilon </math>, where <math>e^{-iHt}</math> is the ideal evolution and <math>||\cdot||</math> is the [[spectral norm]].
A special case of the Hamiltonian simulation problem is the local Hamiltonian simulation problem. This is when <math>H</math> is a k-local Hamiltonian on <math>n</math> qubits where <math>H = \sum_{j \mathop =1}^m H_j </math> and <math>H_j</math> acts [[Triviality (mathematics)|non-trivially]] on at most <math>k</math> qubits instead of <math>n</math> qubits.<ref name=Lloyd1996>{{Cite journal
 | title = Universal quantum simulators
 | year = 1996
 | author = Lloyd, S.
 | journal = Science
 | pages = 1073–8
 | volume = 273
 | issue = 5278
 | doi = 10.1126/science.273.5278.1073
 | pmid = 8688088
|bibcode = 1996Sci...273.1073L | s2cid = 43496899
 }}</ref> The local Hamiltonian simulation problem is important because most Hamiltonians that occur in nature are k-local.<ref name= Lloyd1996/>

== Techniques ==
=== Product formulas ===
{{main|Time-evolving block decimation}}
Also known as [[Lie product formula|Trotter formulas]] or Trotter–Suzuki decompositions, Product formulas simulate the sum-of-terms of a Hamiltonian by simulating each one separately for a small time slice.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1=Suzuki|first1=Masuo| title= General theory of fractal path integrals with applications to many-body theories and statistical physics | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | volume=32| pages=400–407 | year=1991 |issue=2|doi=10.1063/1.529425 |bibcode=1991JMP....32..400S}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berry|first1=Dominic| last2=Ahokas | first2=Graeme | last3=Cleve| first3 =Richard | last4=Sanders | first4= Barry| title= Efficient Quantum Algorithms for Simulating Sparse Hamiltonians| journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics | volume=270| pages=359–371 | year=2007 |issue=2| doi=10.1007/s00220-006-0150-x| arxiv=quant-ph/0508139|bibcode=2007CMaPh.270..359B|s2cid=37923044}}</ref> 
If <math>H = A + B + C </math>, then <math> U = e^{-i(A + B + C)t}</math> is well-approximated by <math>(e^{-iAt/r}e^{-iBt/r}e^{-iCt/r})^r</math> for a large <math>r</math>; where <math>r</math> is the number of time steps to simulate for. The larger the <math>r</math>, the more accurate the simulation. 

If the Hamiltonian is represented as a [[Sparse matrix]], the distributed [[edge coloring]] algorithm can be used to decompose it into a sum of terms; which can then be simulated by a Trotter–Suzuki algorithm.<ref name = walk />


=== Taylor series ===
<math> e^{-iHt} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^ \infty \frac{(-iHt)^{n}}{n!} = I - iHt - \frac{H^{2}t^{2}}{2} + \frac{iH^{3}t^{3}}{6} + \cdots  </math> by the [[Taylor series]] expansion.<ref name = taylor>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1412.4687|last1 = Berry|first1 = Dominic |last2= Childs |first2 = Andrew |last3 = Cleve |first3 = Richard |last4 = Kothari |first4 = Robin| last5 = Somma |first5 =  Rolando  |title = Simulating Hamiltonian dynamics with a truncated Taylor series|journal = Physical Review Letters|volume = 114|issue = 9|article-number = 090502|year = 2015|bibcode = 2015PhRvL.114i0502B|doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.090502|pmid = 25793789|s2cid = 15682119}}</ref> This says that during the evolution of a quantum state, the Hamiltonian is applied over and over again to the system with a various number of repetitions. The first term is the [[identity matrix]] so the system doesn't change when it is applied, but in the second term the Hamiltonian is applied once. For practical implementations, the series has to be truncated <math> \left( \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^N \frac{(-iHt)^{n}}{n!} \right)</math>, where the bigger the <math>N</math>, the more accurate the simulation.<ref name = large /> This truncated expansion is then implemented via the [[linear combination]] of unitaries (LCU) technique for Hamiltonian simulation.<ref name = taylor /> Namely, one decomposes the Hamiltonian <math> H = \sum_{\ell=1}^L \alpha_\ell H_\ell </math> such that each <math> H_\ell </math> is unitary (for instance, the Pauli operators always provide such a basis), and so each <math> H^n = \sum_{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n=1}^L \alpha_{\ell_1} \cdots \alpha_{\ell_n} H_{\ell_1} \cdots H_{\ell_n} </math> is also a linear combination of unitaries.

=== Quantum walk ===
{{main|Quantum walk}}
In the [[quantum walk]], a unitary operation whose spectrum is related to the Hamiltonian is implemented then the [[Quantum phase estimation algorithm]] is used to adjust the eigenvalues. This makes it unnecessary to decompose the Hamiltonian into a sum-of-terms like the Trotter-Suzuki methods.<ref name = taylor />

=== Quantum signal processing ===
{{main|Quantum Signal Processing}}
The quantum signal processing algorithm works by transducing the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian into an ancilla qubit,  transforming the eigenvalues with single qubit rotations and finally projecting the ancilla.<ref name=LC2016>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1606.02685 |last1 = Low|first1 = Guang Hao |last2= Chuang |first2 = Isaac |title = Optimal Hamiltonian Simulation by Quantum Signal Processing|journal = Physical Review Letters|volume = 118|issue = 1|article-number = 010501|year = 2017|bibcode = 2017PhRvL.118a0501L|doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.010501|pmid = 28106413|s2cid = 1118993}}</ref> It has been proved to be optimal in query complexity when it comes to Hamiltonian simulation.<ref name=LC2016/>

== Complexity ==
The table of the complexities of the Hamiltonian simulation algorithms mentioned above. The Hamiltonian simulation can be studied in two ways. This depends on how the Hamiltonian is given. If it is given explicitly, then gate complexity matters more than query complexity. If the Hamiltonian is described as an Oracle ([[black box]]) then the number of queries to the oracle is more important than the gate count of the circuit. The following table shows the gate and query complexity of the previously mentioned techniques.
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Technique
! Gate complexity
! Query complexity
|-
| Product formula 1st order
| <math>O\left(\frac{t^{2}}{\epsilon}\right) </math><ref name = large>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1711.10980 |last1 =Childs|first1 = Andrew |last2= Maslov |first2 =  Dmitri |last3 = Nam |first3 = Yunseong |title = Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup|journal =Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume =115|issue =38|pages =9456–9461|year = 2017|bibcode =2018PNAS..115.9456C|doi =10.1073/pnas.1801723115|pmid =30190433|pmc =6156649|doi-access =free}}</ref>
| <math> O\left(d^{3} t \left(\frac{dt}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}k}\right)</math><ref> {{cite AV media | people=Kothari, Robin | date=Dec 8, 2017 | title=Quantum algorithms for Hamiltonian simulation: Recent results and open problems | medium=Youtube| location=United States | publisher=IBM Research| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PerdRJ-offU}} </ref>
|- 
| Taylor series
| <math>O\left(\frac{t \log^{2}\left(\frac{t}{\epsilon}\right)}{\log \log \frac{t}{\epsilon}}\right) </math><ref name = large/>
| <math> O\left(\frac{d^{2} ||H||_{\rm max} \log{\frac{d^{2} ||H||_{max}}{\epsilon}}}{\log \log{\frac{d^{2} ||H||_{\rm max}}{\epsilon}}}\right) </math><ref name = taylor />
|-
| Quantum walk
| <math>O\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right) </math><ref name = large/>
| <math> O\left(d || H||_{\rm max} \frac{t}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right)</math><ref name = walk>{{Cite book |arxiv = 1501.01715 |last1 = Berry|first1 = Dominic|last2= Childs |first2 = Andrew| last3 = Kothari| first3 = Robin |chapter = Hamiltonian simulation with nearly optimal dependence on all parameters|year = 2015|bibcode = 2015arXiv150101715B|doi = 10.1109/FOCS.2015.54|title = 2015 IEEE 56th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science|pages = 792–809|isbn = 978-1-4673-8191-8|s2cid = 929117}}</ref>
|-
| Quantum signal processing
| <math>O\left(t + \log{\frac{1}{\epsilon}}\right) </math><ref name = large/>
|<math> O\left(t d || H||_{\rm max} + \frac{\log{\frac{1}{\epsilon}}}{\log \log {\frac{1}{\epsilon}}}\right) </math><ref name=LC2016 />
|}
Where <math>||H||_{\rm max}</math> is the largest entry of <math>H</math>.
